claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
Retention of a single-phase solid solution is governed primarily by the balance between configurational entropy and lattice strain.
Lattice strain in these alloys arises from differences in atomic size among their constituent metals.
High configurational entropy favors retention of a disordered, single-phase state.
Elevated operating temperatures increase the importance of configurational-entropy stabilization.
If configurational entropy sufficiently counters lattice strain, phase segregation will not occur.
If lattice strain overcomes entropy stabilization, the solid solution will undergo phase segregation and decomposition.
Nanoparticles with relatively high configurational entropy and low lattice strain will retain their solid-solution structure during operation.
Nanoparticles with relatively high configurational entropy and low lattice strain will maintain stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Larger atomic-size disparities will produce greater lattice strain.
Samples with greater lattice strain will exhibit more phase separation.
Phase separation will cause corresponding changes in catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
At sufficiently low temperatures, strain effects will not be induced.
An inert atmosphere can prevent a reactive driving force for phase segregation.
New XRD peaks or distinct phase domains in TEM constitute evidence of phase segregation.

contradictions.description: The conditions frame inert-atmosphere samples at the same temperatures as the controlled comparison for evaluating the prediction, while the boundary states that deviations are expected in inert atmospheres because they prevent a reactive driving force. This makes it unclear whether the entropy–strain prediction is intended to apply to the inert controls.

The central hypothesis presents entropy–strain balance as the primary governor of stability, whereas the boundary introduces reactive chemistry as a potentially necessary driving force for segregation. The relative roles of these two proposed controls are not reconciled.
